Good evening, everyone. This is Patricia Lowe, your property manager, with a short update before Tuesday's annual meeting. First, the roof. As you know, the repair cost two hundred thousand dollars. If the building had saved more in past years, the reserve fund would be healthy today, and nobody would be paying a special assessment. The new board will have to fix that. Second, the pool. We have received bids from three new contractors. The cheapest one can start in November. I know it's frustrating. If we had chosen a contractor with better references last spring, the pool would be open right now. Third, the election. Two seats are open on the board, and owners can be nominated at the meeting. And please, if you can't come, sign a proxy. Last year we didn't have a quorum, and that's why the bylaws are still not updated. See you on Tuesday at seven, in the lobby lounge.

Hi, I'm Tom. Three years ago I joined the board of my building, and I made almost every mistake a new member can make. My first mistake was simple: I didn't read the bylaws. If I had read them, I would have known that the board can't spend more than fifty thousand dollars without a vote of the owners. I approved a new gym, and we had to cancel the contract. My second mistake was trying to do everything alone. Today I'm a better board member, because I ask questions before I vote. If I were starting today, I would do three things. I'd read the bylaws in the first week. I'd meet the property manager before the first meeting. And I'd talk to the owners who never come, because they're the people who send a proxy and then complain. Being on a board isn't a title. It's a job, and nobody pays you to do it. But if more good people ran for their boards, our buildings would be much better places to live.
